speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday during the debate on the budget I raised certain points with regard to Canadian representation at a number of conferences; and as reported at page 2373 of Hansard I said:
But I wonder how important to the government and the people of Canada was a conference described as the international congress of chocolate and cocoa manufacturers which was held at Lausanne last year.
Then further on I said:
And I do not know that we have heard anything of what was gained by our attendance at the international congress of psychiatrists at Paris, or the meeting of the directing council and sanitary conference of the Pan-American bureau of Ciudad Trujillo.
Later I referred to the Washington conference of the society of vertebrate palaeontology and the palaeontological society. At that point I noticed that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) was about to rise, and I mentioned that fact. Then, as reported in Hansard, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
I was just going to say there were no delegations at those conferences.
It is possible that there is some distinction in the use of words which is in the mind of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but certainly the thought conveyed to my mind, and I know to others, was that this statement was incorrect as to the fact that Canada had attended those conferences. I therefore should like to refer to the report of the Department of External Affairs for the year 1950, issued over the signature of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. At pages 82 and 83 I find that Canada was represented, according to the official statement of the department, at the conferences which I have just mentioned.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: COST OF CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON APRIL 25
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I
should like to add a word on the question of privilege raised by the hon. gentleman. If my intervention yesterday gave the impression, as it might well have done, that there 80709-1534
was no Canadian representation of any kind at these conferences, I was entirely wrong, and I apologize to the hon. gentleman and to the house for giving that impression. It is quite true that, with regard to these four conferences, there were individual Canadian observers at two of them and individual Canadian representatives from departments of government at the other two. In that sense, Mr. Speaker, Canada was represented at those four meetings; and I am extremely sorry to have given the wrong impression by my intervention yesterday.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: RETALIATORY MEASURES IN THE EVENT OP BOMBING FROM MANCHURIAN BASES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has Canada, as a participant in military action in Korea and as a member of the United Nations, been consulted regarding the announcement that enemy air bases in Manchuria will be attacked if the Chinese communists use heavy air power against United Nations troops? If so, will the minister make a statement in this connection?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RETALIATORY MEASURES IN THE EVENT OP BOMBING FROM MANCHURIAN BASES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in reply to the important point raised by the hon. member, I would say that so far as the government is aware, no announcement on the subject has been made. The hon. member is presumably referring to a report in this morning's newspapers which is attributed to a spokesman for the United States delegation at Lake Success.

subtopic: RETALIATORY MEASURES IN THE EVENT OP BOMBING FROM MANCHURIAN BASES
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RETALIATORY MEASURES IN THE EVENT OP BOMBING FROM MANCHURIAN BASES
speechtext:
However, 1 am very glad to have this opportunity of making a brief statement of the government's position in regard to this matter.
Some five months ago the government informed the United States government, in response to an inquiry from that government-they brought the matter up-that, though a strong case could be made under international law that the United Nations commander in chief had the right to retaliate against any air attacks launched from Manchuria, we considered it important, as indeed did other governments, that no military operations take place outside Korean borders without specific authority from the United Nations.
Since that time various aspects of the Korean operations have been the subject of discussions in Washington, as indeed I have indicated previously in the house, among representatives of the countries having forces in Korea.
So far, however, the Canadian government has received no request for concurrence in any proposal to authorize United Nations retaliation upon enemy air bases outside Korea, probably for the very good reason that there has been no massive enemy air

bombing from Manchuria. If there is such air intervention, for the consequences of which the Chinese communists would have to bear full responsibility, it is our view that those countries with forces in Korea, and participating in military operations there, should be consulted in regard to the implications of that action-that is, air bombing- and in regard to any retaliatory action which may be required to meet it.
However, it is of course possible to visualize a situation where immediate retaliatory action, without consultation, might be unavoidable in pursuing enemy bombers back to the Manchurian air base from which they came. The decision on the spot to take such immediate retaliatory action would presumably be based on overriding considerations of military security.
In any discussions regarding more general retaliatory action against Manchurian air bases, the decision to authorize such action would, as we see it, have to balance very carefully local military considerations against the risk of precipitating a further extension of the war and the effect of such an extension on the security of the United Nations forces in Korea, and the accomplishment of United Nations aims there.

subtopic: RETALIATORY MEASURES IN THE EVENT OP BOMBING FROM MANCHURIAN BASES
speechtext: Is there any continuing conference of representatives of nations whose forces are engaged in Korea, through which these matters can be cleared at very short notice; or do they have to go through the long procedure of conferring among the governments of the various countries?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RETALIATORY MEASURES IN THE EVENT OP BOMBING FROM MANCHURIAN BASES
speechtext:
No; the representatives of
governments contributing forces to the Korean campaign meet almost daily in Washington, and on a level high enough to make it possible to get a decision almost immediately in respect of these matters.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE OF FAMILY INCOME SPENT ON MAJOR CONSUMER ITEMS SUBJECT TO SALES TAX FOR VARIOUS INCOME GROUPS
speechtext:
I wonder how the department can perform its function in connection with the preparation of the budget each year, or advise the minister or the budget committee as to what steps should be taken with reference to expanding the exemptions from the sales tax, unless there is a break-down indicating the amount levied on various staple commodities. We all know that clothing of practically every kind1 is subject to sales tax. Boots and shoes are subject to sales tax. The clothing that all of us are wearing in this house this afternoon has been subject to sales tax if produced in Canada. I must express some surprise that it is not possible for the government to acquaint the house with the amount realized from this tax on staple necessities of that kind.
It is because the tax applies heavily, and will hereafter apply more heavily, to staple necessities of life that we in the opposition have been so firm in our denunciation of this increase. At a time when inflation and the soaring cost of living have laid burdens upon people of slender means which under present conditions they are simply not able to bear, the imposition of an increased burden of this kind on the very necessities of life is worthy only of denunciation at the hands of members who are vigilant to do their duty in the face of the difficulties under which so many Canadians are labouring today in making ends meet.
I have mentioned the clothing that we wear, the shoes on our feet. There are many other necessities of life the cost of which is going to be severely increased as a result of this further imposition by way of sales tax. I gave a simple illustration the other day, the scribblers, pencils and things of that nature that school children are going to have

to buy. In. some municipalities these articles are provided by the boards of education at the expense of the local taxpayers. What justification can there be for the federal government to increase impositions of that kind on such necessities, the cost of which is borne either by the parents of school children or by municipal taxpayers who have to provide the means out of which boards of education purchase these necessities? What justification can there be for the federal government to tax local governments in that way? It seems to me that a government at Ottawa that proceeds on that basis has chosen a course that cannot be condoned by the House of Commons.
This present budget resolution, perhaps above all budget resolutions that have provoked a storm of public protest, stands out as the one which has provoked the greatest measure of protest and consternation throughout the country. Others, of course, share the unenviable distinction of this resolution in heaping further burdens upon the shoulders of those who can barely stagger along now in view of the soaring cost of the necessities of life. This has the peculiar distinction of being the one which perhaps more clearly than any other offends against all the rules of budgeting that should be followed at a time like this. That is because it applies to consumers, since there is very little choice with respect to many of the commodities to which the sales tax applies. So many of those commodities, according to any civilized standard, any Canadian standard, cannot be regarded as anything but the accepted necessities of life.
This is the kind of tax that was denounced in a general election campaign ten years ago by the late Mr. Mackenzie King, who went up and down this country calling it an iniquitous tax. Yet this is the tax which in this year 1951 the Minister of Finance has chosen not simply to continue, but to increase by a further twenty-five per cent. We know things change in the Liberal party. We know they have changed drastically when we recall what was said on the subject of the sales^ tax by previous ministers of finance. I am sure I need not repeat the pertinent reference to the sales tax made by the late Mr. Ralston in his budget speech in 1940, the first year of the war. I am sure I need not repeat what was said on this very subject by Mr. Ilsley in wartime, and again in peacetime, in 1945. Faced with the need for increased revenue, they deliberately and purposely declined to increase the sales tax. The need for revenue was very great in the years of which I am speaking. The government claims that its need for revenue today is great. Some of us might feel more certain that the need is

genuinely great if the government were not so averse to permitting any effective scrutiny of the estimates of expenditure they have asked the house to vote. Having tied the hands of the house, having prevented the house from conducting any really effective scrutiny of the estimates of expenditure, the government has deliberately invited suspicion in this house and throughout the country as to whether these gigantic increases in taxes really are necessary.
In any case, whether any increase in taxation is necessary, this is the last place it should have been imposed. If the government seriously appreciated the problem of inflation, if it understood how inflation hurts Canadians from coast to coast in trying to meet their family budgets from day to day, one would have expected a resolute effort to be made to reduce this tax which does so much to increase the cost of living. Those of us who three years ago had to sit through the agonizing experience of the special committee on prices will have some recollection that a good deal of evidence was presented to show that prices were rising and imposing a very heavy burden upon the average Canadian family just because the government was applying taxes of this kind. And those taxes, including the sales tax, are not applied only to luxuries, if you please, but in many cases to commodities which under any accepted Canadian standard are basic necessities of life. In the face of all that, however, the government chooses not to reduce the tax or even to leave it at its previous high level, but to increase it. The present minister has chosen to disregard the words of, and ignore the course followed by, his predecessors, Mr. Ralston and Mr. Ilsley. In the war years and in 1945 the need for revenue was greater, as far as finances were concerned, than is the need of the minister today; none the less they deliberately refused to increase this tax.
It was not that the tax was not easily collected. As a matter of fact, in his budget speech of 1945 Mr. Ilsley referred to the fact that the tax was very easy to collect. Therefore it is the kind of tax that might be expected to appeal to a minister of finance who was not concerned with anything more than the ease with which he and his tax collectors could put their hands into the pockets of the people and withdraw the needed revenue. Those previous ministers, faced with that problem, chose not to increase the sales tax. The present minister, faced with a similar problem, nevertheless now comes forward with a proposal that the tax be increased by a thumping twenty-five per cent. I say there is no justification whatsoever for this budget resolution. I should have thought this would
Excise Tax Act
have been one opportunity for private members supporting the government in this house, concerned as they surely must be with the problems being faced by Canadians in trying to meet their family budgets, to rise in their places and say: We cannot support an increase in the sales tax when we know what further burdens it is certain to impose upon Canadian families.
We will listen attentively for some evidence that the pleas of the people, particularly those of small means who by the tens of thousands in all parts of this country are barely keeping their heads above water in the face of the soaring costs of the necessities of life, have made some impression upon the private members in this house who support the government.
What does this mean? The tax does not mean just 10 per cent. We have been faced before with this question of what this tax really does mean in terms of what the consumer must pay. It is levied on the producer or manufacturer because that is where it is easiest for the government to collect it. That is the one reason why this tax is imposed at that stage of the process by which goods are fabricated and made available to the consumer. It is easy for the government to collect. It is easy to administer. It is easy to enforce. They are not dealing with so many people at that stage of production and marketing. For that reason the tax is imposed at the source; and there it is carefully hidden. But as you know, Mr. Speaker, every time a commodity passes from one hand to another the tax acts like a snowball. It attracts mark-ups at every stage. I am not going to inflict upon hon. members the example I have given previously, but you will find in a simple case where the commodity passes through only three hands, from producer to wholesaler, who adds his 10 per cent mark-up, from wholesaler to retailer, who adds his 50 per cent mark-up, and then directly into the hands of the consumer, that the tax previously amounted to not 8 per cent, but 14-4 per cent, when the consumer had to pay it. Now the tax is 10 per cent at the source, and in that simple illustration by the time it reaches the consumer it amounts to 18 per cent, which is a nice round figure. If this afternoon this house approves this budget resolution and it becomes law, this house is not increasing the tax on these necessities of life simply by 2 per cent. In even the simplest case it is increasing the tax by no less than 3 [DOT] 6 per cent. That is the simple situation. We are invited by this government, in the simplest case, the case that costs the consumer the least, to boost a tax on the consumer up to 18 per cent.

Excise Tax Act
Anyone who is looking around seriously for reasons why the cost of living is high today cannot fail to stop in the first place at this sales tax. The Minister of Finance can talk until he is black in the face about this international phenomenon of inflation, but he cannot change the basic fact that this government is the big factor in creating inflation in this country today. Anyone in this house who is looking about seriously for a means of reducing the soaring cost of living to make it a little bit easier for people to meet their budgets will start right here. He will begin by refusing to support this iniquitous resolution, this tax that is doubly iniquitous because the proposal is to increase a tax that sixteen years ago Mr. Mackenzie King denounced up and down the country as iniquitous. What would he say today, sixteen years later?
In 1935, sir, the problem was not one of high prices. The principal problem in 1935 was one of low prices to the producer. It would have been relatively an easy matter then to say, if Mr. Mackenzie King had chosen to do so: Oh, well, this does not add very much to the cost of living; this does not take very much out of the pockets of the people, because prices are so low. What is the situation in 1951? If this tax was iniquitous in 1935, then this increase is an infamous proposal to put before the House of Commons and the people of Canada today a :25 per cent increase applying to so many .things that are basic necessities of life.
It seems to me, sir, that this resolution is as clear a test as this house is likely to face, at this or any other session of parliament, as to just how serious each individual member is on this subject of concern for the lot of the Canadian family in meeting its budget in the light of the way the rising cost of living has torn that budget to shreds and tatters in hundreds of thousands of cases. Here is a simple test every member of this house will be called upon to face. I hope there will be full opportunity given and taken, when you call finally for a vote on this particular resolution in this committee or elsewhere, for members to indicate- every one on his own personal responsibility, regardless of whether or not he is a supporter of the government-whether he is really serious in expressing his concern for the problem faced by the average Canadian family with respect to the high cost of living today. I believe, sir, that to a degree rarely existing in this House of Commons, every member is on trial this afternoon, placed there by this first resolution.

I join with my hon. friend in supporting the propriety of these sections being voted upon separately. The citation to which he refers reads:
A motion which contains two or more distinct propositions may be divided so that the sense of the house may be taken on each separately.
If that were not so then the house would simply be in the position of an automaton carrying out everything the government wanted done, whether certain things contained in a resolution were acceptable or not. Surely parliament is not to be emasculated in that way. The section of the resolution in question reads:
1. That the rate of the general sales tax be increased from eight to ten per cent and that the

rate of sales tax on those articles at present subject to four per cent be increased to five per cent.
Then the next section provides for an increase of the excise tax on goods mentioned in schedule I of the act, the increase being from 15 per cent to 25 per cent. The next section provides that the excise tax on candy and so on be reduced from 30 to 15 per cent.
If the proposition were accepted that the house could not vote on these items individually, no matter how many in the house were opposed to No. 1, the purpose for which parliament exists and this committee is constituted would be entirely denied. After all, rules are made in order to expedite the fullest possible discussion consistent with the exigencies of parliamentary debate. The citation has never been changed. The need for such a citation and the propriety of the course being followed of each item being voted on individually is clear from a mere consideration of what the result would be if such were not the fact.
Parliament would be placed in this position. The government could place in its motion five or six items that were acceptable and one item that no hon. member in the house would accept, and yet the committee would be denied the opportunity of saying whether each particular section was proper and whether any particular section was not proper. In other words, if the contention of the parliamentary assistant be correct,, we are in the position of simply having to take everything that the government hands out without the opportunity of voting on those things that we believe are not proper. I submit that ordinary reason and ordinary common sense supports the citation to which reference has been made.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, now that the vote has been taken I should like to say a few words on section 1 of the resolution. I am unalterably opposed to the general sales tax, including the 25 per cent increase proposed in section 1 of the resolution, for five specific reasons. I am not going to repeat the arguments I put forward during the budget debate, but I do intend to outline again the five bases upon which I have taken my position.
I am opposed to the general sales tax and the increase proposed in section 1 of the resolution because this tax increases the cost of living burden upon the lower income groups of our Canadian people. That group

of people are already overburdened by a heavy cost of living which is continually increasing.
In the second place, I am opposed to the tax because it pyramids prices and makes it necessary for consumers to pay more in increased prices than is collected by the government in the form of revenue. I have already presented evidence by authorities who have investigated our Canadian sales tax and who show that often the consumer has to pay as much as 40 per cent more in increased prices than the government receives by way of revenue. This is iniquitous taxation; it is what the hon. member for Eglinton refers to as infamous and I do not support it for one moment, as* I have shown already by my vote.
The third reason why I am opposed to it is that the sales tax is inflationary. In times like these it aggravates a condition of inflation that is already very serious. On numerous occasions during the past several months the government has been asked by the people of Canada to take action to curb inflationary pressures. They had every reason to believe that the government would take such action during the present session. They looked to the budget as one place where relief perhaps could be given, but instead of any relief from inflationary pressures the government now proposes to impose a tax that is definitely inflationary, and there is no one who can prove that it is not.
The reason that I am opposed to the proposition of an increased sales tax is that the general sales tax is a hidden tax. I have always been opposed to hidden taxes because they take away from the taxpayers of the country any means by which they can gauge the effectiveness of the administration. There is only one way by which the ordinary taxpayer can judge whether a government is efficient and that is by the level of taxes. That is the barometer, and unless that level or barometer is plainly visible the people have no way whatever of knowing about the efficiency or inefficiency of the government. I am suggesting that one of the reasons why this government has attempted on several occasions to convert perfectly visible taxes into hidden taxes is that they want to hide inefficiency, and there is no one who can possibly present a case to disprove that statement. If so, I should like to have them try.
All information about the effect of the imposition of the sales tax has been hidden as well. The government has never attempted at any time to investigate the effect of the incidence of the sales tax upon the economy

to show whether or not there are adverse effects. We have called for it time after time in the name of the people. Ever since I came to this house in 1945 in nearly every session I have pleaded with the government to appoint some sort of commission to investigate the effect upon the Canadian economy of the incidence of the various taxes they are imposing so that we cam see what these effects are, and if they are adverse take action to remove these taxes and to correct the situation. I am asking that the Department of Finance, which is the proper department to do the job, should immediately appoint a commission to make a thorough investigation of the whole hidden tax situation. Let the country know exactly what are the effects of the imposition of the sales tax and other excise taxes.
The fifth reason why I am unalterably opposed to the imposition of this tax is that in many ways it increases the cost of production. However the argument may be presented, the fact remains that certain articles of machinery and certain tools used in the process of production, the many automobiles that are used in the process of production, the trucks that enter into the process of production, the clothing worn by labourers in producing things, and I could go on and name a number of other things, are affected by this tax. Therefore the prices of these articles will be increased if this imposition is passed and made law. That will inevitably increase the cost of production and further add to the inflationary situation in this country.
These are the five important reasons why I feel that it is unwise and iniquitous for the government to propose an increase in the sales tax particularly at this time when the people of the country are crying out against the terrible cost of living, when hundreds of thousands of our people, with all their backlog of wartime savings melted away, are just beginning to feel the pinch. People with children going to school cannot possibly get the vitamins and the food required to maintain the health of their children simply because of these iniquitous hidden taxes. I have had some experience with sales taxes, and my experience was not a very happy one. I administered the sales tax in the province of Alberta when I became provincial treasurer there, and I might state for the information of hon. members that after some little experience with it I decided it should be abolished. I did abolish it in 1937, and I have been opposed to such taxes ever since because I know something about what they
Excise Tax Act
do to people and how difficult this type of impost is to administer.
I sat and listened to the crossfire that took place when my friend the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was speaking. Certain members to my right and across the floor accused the Saskatchewan government of imposing a sales tax. They spoke as if that was every reason why the Liberal government should be supported in increasing the sales tax. Let me point out that there is quite a difference between the two taxes. The so-called sales tax imposed in the province of Saskatchewan is not properly a general sales tax at all. It is an ultimate purchaser's tax which is imposed at the consumer level as a straight percentage of the retail price to the consumer. When the consumer purchases the item he knows exactly what the cost ex tax is and he knows what the cost with tax is. That is an ultimate purchaser's tax. I am surprised that was not mentioned in the crossfire that took place because it is certainly an entirely different situation.
I think it is somewhat of an act of salvation that the provinces have not the right to impose sales taxes at the manufacturer's level. I am very happy that they have not. Certainly the people of Canada ought to be able to know exactly what they are paying in the form of taxes. If a system can be worked out at any time by which people will know when they buy an article how much they are paying in actual cost and how much they are paying in actual tax, I think it ought to be done. Such a system should be introduced.
I have taken part in the proceedings this afternoon with my vote. I have done all I can in a constitutional way, and so have my colleagues, to eliminate this vicious thing in order to protect the Canadian people who have not asked for this tax and in fact have demanded that it be not imposed. As I say, we have taken every constitutional means within our power thus far, but I am suggesting that, in spite of the overriding attitude and power of a power-drunk government, there is a remedy, and the opposition can apply that remedy. I suggest that we can prevent the government from putting this thing through. All we have to do is to fight and be ready to stand up here and talk this thing out. If the sixty or more members of the opposition will get their fighting clothes on and each one of them make a forty minute speech or two against it, we can at least hold this thing up until the people of Canada have a chance to tell the government that they had better remove the iniquitous thing or get out and let someone else come in who will do a decent job for them.

Excise Tax Act
If we have any intestinal fortitude on this side of the house that is exactly the sort of thing we will do. I suggest that is the remedy we have to apply against a party and a government that would override the wishes of the people as wantonly as this government does. I know my party are quite ready to do that very thing. As far as we are concerned it is the only remedy left to us. We are proposing to speak just as often as we possibly can, and if the opposition will band together I believe we can keep the government here until next Christmas and prevent this thing from being passed.

speechtext:
I believe I shall discuss the whole resolution at once, and not merely a section or two at a time. The thing that puzzles me, and I think it is puzzling the people of Canada, is that ever since I have been in the house the Liberal party has bitterly denounced the policy of inflation as being a dishonest policy, as being a policy
Excise Tax Act
which steals the savings of the people without disclosing it. And now the government has adopted this policy. They have adopted this policy as a means of bringing in a greater amount of revenue. As a result of this policy there will be an increase in the price of many commodities, and to that extent the policy is inflationary. True, it will bring increased revenue to the government, .and no doubt the government hopes, as a result of the increase in prices, that there will be a reduction in the demand for goods from current income. Even though there may be a reduction in the demand from current income, the minister knows very well that it may not necessarily mean a reduction in demand because, instead of that, people will save that much less. People will also use their savings of the past in order to finance current expenditures.
I noticed a press dispatch in the Ottawa Journal of April 24 which is headed "Inflationary trend seen in new taxes bank review says". It reads:
The current "Business Review" of the Bank of Montreal says that the new taxes provided in the federal budget will doubtless supply funds for soaring defence expenditures, but it finds in them possible inflationary influences.
It adds:	"To point out these difficulties is not
to suggest that practical alternatives were readily available."
The analysis says in part: "In theory it is possible to limit or reduce the level of consumption, in real terms, by budgetary measures operating on the incomes and spending propensities of individuals in the mass.
"But in practice the actual results may be greatly modified by public reaction and the bargaining power of organized groups. For example, the new surtax on incomes will, at midyear, have the initial effect of reducing the take-home pay of that proportion-probably less than half-of the working force now on the income tax roll.
"To some extent the increased tax is as likely to be met by a reduction in savings as by diminished consumption. Moreover, the likelihood of the restraining effect of the tax being in large part offset by subsequent additions to take-home pay is considerable.
"The new indirect taxes-i.e., the increased sales tax and the specific excise taxes1-are, in an economic sense, designed' as a penalty on spending. The imposts will emerge as increases in the prices of the articles affected, with the possibility of the increases in many instances being 'pyramided' by the mark-ups applied by intermediaries between manufacturer and consumer.
"Beyond the range of necessities it is, of course, the option of the consumer to refrain from purchasing the affected articles. But in any event the higher prices will in due course be incorporated into the cost of living index, which is not only the reference point to which basic wage rates are contractually tied in some industries, but which is also a significant symbol indicating, in the eyes of the public at large, the degree to which demands for higher pay are automatically justified . . .
"In the ultimate analysis the effectiveness of budgetary measures as a curb on consumer spending depends on the willingness of the public to permit its spending to be curbed rather than to seek compensatory pay increases."

Excise Tax Act
As is pointed out there, as a result of the increase in the cost of living, the result will probably be a demand right across the country for an increase in wages, which will still further increase the inflationary pressure in this country. I would agree, perhaps, that in so far as a long-term policy is concerned, the budget resolutions may tend to reduce purchases by increasing the cost of living; but whatever the long-range policy may be the immediate effect is to increase prices by an amount at least equivalent to the amount of the sales tax or excise tax. The actual amount of the increase will be greater than the amount of the sales tax because it will be pyramided in mark-ups.
I wonder if the parliamentary assistant would admit that the result of this policy will be to tax the savings of the people in the lower income groups and in the moderate income groups? It will not be a tax on the savings of the people in the higher income brackets, because they will have enough current income to meet the current costs of the goods they buy. But there are many people in the lower income groups who cannot meet the cost of living from their income, and who will therefore have to use their savings. In reality this is in part a hidden tax on the savings of the people in the lower income group.

speechtext:
Just before six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I had been pointing out that for many years now the government has been warning of the dangers of inflation and stressing the fact that a policy of inflation is a policy of dishonesty, a policy under which in reality the savings of the people are filched away. I therefore deplore the fact that the government has now come to the conclusion that it is necessary for them to adopt that same dishonest policy which they have so severely condemned in the past. I quoted from the current review of the Bank of Montreal, which showed clearly and unmistakably that the result of this present budget policy was bound to be one of inflation, or at least that it had highly inflationary tendencies and would probably lead to an all-round increase of wages, which would mean a still further increase in prices.
I also pointed out that one of the most unfortunate results of this policy is that people in the low income groups are not

able to meet the present high cost of living out of their current income and therefore, where they have any savings or any capital, they are drawing on those savings or on that capital in order to supplement their income for the purpose of meeting the high cost of living; and of course they are having to pay these taxes out of those savings. Hence this policy of the government actually is a concealed tax on the savings of the people in the lower income groups. It will not affect the savings of the people in the higher income groups to the same extent, because they will be able to live on current income; but the people in the low income groups who are fortunate enough to have savings will have to utilize them and then pay these taxes.
Many people across the country are wondering how it is that the government is still refusing to take any direct action to control prices. I have come to the conclusion that the government is not interested in reducing prices for the simple reason that they realize that the higher prices go, the higher will be their revenue at any given level of taxation; that is to say, they can get an increase in revenue without increasing taxation so long as they allow prices to rise. In that way they get more revenue and let the people blame industry for the increase in the cost of living instead of themselves accepting a large part of that responsibility.
I think it is generally understood that in normal times high taxation will cause demand for goods to fall off; and as you have demand falling off, unemployment increases and prices fall. That is the orthodox idea and that is, I think we will all agree, what happens in what you might call normal times. But these are not normal times. Already they have been referred to as times of emergency. We therefore realize today that any slackening in internal demand will be taken up by increased external demand and that therefore, instead of demand falling off and unemployment increasing, external demand will take the place of internal demand and keep demand high, and the inflationary pressure will continue even with the increased prices for goods.
How long can we expect this situation to continue? The government appears to look upon it as a temporary situation, or perhaps I should say they hope that it is a temporary situation; because the Minister of Finance stated that perhaps next session they may have to bring in other measures.
What is likely to be the future situation? There are one or two alternatives. The cold war may continue. If the cold war continues, it means we are going to have

continued high expenditures for defence. The Minister of Trade and Commerce I think made that quite clear when he spoke. So long as we continue to have high expenditures for defence, there will of course be a heavy demand for materials manufactured in Canada. In addition, so long as this cold war continues there will be, for food produced in Canada, a heavy demand by members of the North Atlantic treaty and also by various countries in Asia that we are obliged to support under the United Nations organization. If therefore we are going to continue to have the cold war for the next five or six years, we are going to continue to have inflationary pressure.

That the rate of the general sales tax be increased from eight to ten per cent and that the rate of sales tax on those articles at present subject to four per cent be increased to five per cent.
It was suggested that that tax should be eliminated; and the parliamentary assistant, among others, suggested that any time we advocated the elimination of a tax we should suggest an alternative. When the leader of this group spoke he mentioned that as an alternative there could be an increase in the tax on liquor. The Minister of Finance has argued that if we have an increase in the tax on liquor at this time we may very well reach the law of diminishing return. Well, if we reach the law of diminishing return, so far as liquor is concerned, would that not be a worth-while objective? Is the government going to take the stand that it wants to increase the consumption of liquor in this country? Would they not actually be doing something for the welfare and health of the people of Canada if, as a result of a tax on liquor, there was a reduction in the consumption of liquor in this country?
Therefore if an increase in taxation in this regard would have that result-and I am not saying that it would-but if such an increase in taxation would have that result, namely that it would reduce the consumption of liquor, then I would say we would be achieving a worth-while objective. Then, again, if the minister thinks an increase in the price of liquor would reduce the demand for it, and feels that in order to maintain the revenue from that source he would like to have an increase rather than a decrease in consumption, I suggest all that would be necessary would be to maintain the price of liquor at the present level and then increase the water content in each bottle. A person .would still be able to buy a bottle of liquor for the same price-but perhaps it would be a bottle with less kick. Some might say it would be less effective-but there, again, it is a matter of opinion. It might have less effect upon the person who drank it but the person would remain more effective than if the water content had not been increased.
I take the odd drink, but it would not worry me very much if such drinks were eliminated entirely. But I have seen strange consequences as a result of an over-indulgence in liquor. My mind always goes back to the

Excise Tax Act
last war when, one day, coming back from the front line, I came across one of my platoon commanders very busily shooting at a bath-mat. I know what he thought he was doing: he thought he was shooting rats. I was afraid he might mistake one of my feet for a rat, so I went ini the other direction. But the strange thing was that the next day that man did not remember having shot at imaginary rats; he had forgotten all about it. But he was having a fine time with his hunting expedition on rats-I suggest he would have been no worse off if he had not been able to get that liquor so as to indulge in his hunting spree. Some people are not satisfied with shooting rats; they go after pink elephants. If we were to put more water in the liquor they would probably be satisfied with mice, instead of elephants. I do not think it would be detrimental to the country if an increase in the taxation on liquor had the effect of reducing consumption. Indeed I believe it would be a good thing and would be beneficial to the country. The man with money, who wanted liquor, could still get it; people with less money would probably drink beer, and perhaps they would be better off. But it certainly does not worry me at all when the minister argues that an increase in the tax on liquor would curtail consumption, because I believe that would be a beneficial result.
Then the next paragraph in the resolution states:
That the excise tax on goods mentioned in schedule I of the act, and on furs, that are at present subject to the rate of fifteen per cent be increased to twenty-five per cent.
I understand this includes radios, household electrical appliances, cameras, cosmetics, cars and the like. I believe the minister has referred to most of those articles as being articles of luxury. And what about the working man who resides several miles from the city, and has to drive several miles to town so as to engage in his work? To that man a motor car is absolutely essential so that he may go to his job. Certainly the minister cannot argue, in the light of those facts, that a car is a luxury. It may be used as a luxury by some people; but to other people it is a piece of equipment that is absolutely essential to the jobs in which they are engaged.
Then, of course, those who use cars as a luxury would be able to buy them, despite the amount of the tax. It is the people in the lower income groups who will find it difficult to buy new cars, in the light of these taxes. No doubt some people will argue, "Well, people in lower income groups should not buy new cars; they should buy old cars." I am sure there are many hon. members who at some time or other have bought an old car, and have realized that old cars are not always the cheapest things to buy. Sometimes it is cheaper to buy a new one, because tremendous repair bills may pile up so that an old car becomes a liability rather than an asset-and people on low incomes are not in a position to afford heavy repair bills.
I know as a matter of fact farmers often find it is actually cheaper to trade in machinery after a few years; it is cheaper in time saved and cheaper from the standpoint of saving repair bills.

Then the fourth paragraph is in these words:
That there be imposed, levied and collected1 an excise tax of fifteen per cent on the following goods when adapted to household or apartment use:
(a) stoves, hot plates, grills and other appliances when adapted wholly or in part for cooking and when designed for using other than solid fuels;
As has been pointed out, while this does not include stoves that burn coal or wood, it does include electric stoves and gas stoves. Many houses are designed so that only gas or electric stoves can be used in them. Therefore it would be a hardship to people starting up in houses of that kind if they have to pay this tax on that type of stove.
Then the paragraph includes washing machines operated by electric or other power. I cannot understand how the Minister of Finance can possibly in any way regard a washing machine as a luxury. Wealthy people do not use them; they send their washing out, or at least most of them do. I suppose some of them use washing machines. But people who do their washing at home must have washing machines; I think all will agree on that. We do not expect them to use the washboard in these days. Because of this provision, and this additional tax, it will be more expensive for them to buy washing machines. Perhaps the minister wants people to stop using soap, because some of the ingredients of soap can be used in munitions.
The next paragraph reads:
(c) electric, gas or kerosene refrigerators and freezing equipment and complete parts therefor including coils, condensing or compressor units motors, cabinets, boxes, evaporators and expansion valves.
I can easily understand how many people would regard a refrigerator as a luxury, but on the other hand a refrigerator is a necessity in homes without basements if they are to eliminate spoilage. With the present high cost of food people cannot afford to have their purchases spoil and therefore a refrigerator is a necessity. Wartime houses have been built without basements, and certainly with a climate such as we have here in the summertime a refrigerator is a necessity if there is no basement. In western Canada many people live nine, ten, fifteen or twenty miles from town and they have to buy from week to week. In hot weather they find it hard to keep their food without a refrigerator.
I admit we have done it in the past, but in those days prices were not as high as they are today.
Apparently the Minister of Finance feels that the people who want these things should be prepared to wait. How long should people wait for these things? Is there any
Excise Tax Act
likelihood that prices will fall in the near future? During the last war and after the last war the people of Canada were asked to co-operate by refraining from buying these things I have referred to, things that were perhaps not considered to be absolutely essential. The Minister of Finance asked the people to stop spending their money on these things, to put it into bonds, and then later when prices had fallen and the goods were in more plentiful supply they would be in position to buy them. Many people co-operated with the government. Here is what the Minister of Finance said, as reported on page 1800 of Hansard of April 10, 1951:
We in Canada have already done a great deal. As I have said on previous occasions, this is not a matter in which government policies alone can provide a complete solution. It is a matter which requires the fullest co-operation of all sections and groups, in which every person has a part to play.
As I was pointing out, in the past many people did co-operate with the government. Those who co-operated by refraining from buying these things are the people who got it in the neck. The people who said, "Oh, to heck, with the government, I am going to buy a new refrigerator or a new stove or a new car," probably were able to buy forty per cent cheaper than they could today. The people who took to heart what the government was saying, that they should refrain from buying these things; those who said, "All right, we will co-operate, we will wait until they are more plentiful," found after they had waited two or three years that prices have continuously risen. Some stepped in at that time, but others kept on waiting and some are still waiting. Now they have either to continue waiting or if they want to buy, they must pay the already high prices plus this fifteen per cent excise tax.
How can the government expect co-operation from the people when they break faith in this way? Those people who listened to the government expected the government to play their part in keeping prices down. But those people who refrained from buying at the request of the government are now faced with greatly increased prices, plus this additional tax.
The people who are probably the hardest hit, the people for whom the Minister of Veterans Affairs should feel especially concerned, and I am sure he is, are the veterans.
I recall how at the end of the last war the Minister of Finance referred to the fact that after world war I there had been inflation, prices had gone up and the veterans coming home had to pay greatly inflated prices for the things they required. The former minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, said that they did not intend to allow that situation to develop

Excise Tax Act
after the second world war. He said that they were not going to have the war veterans coming home and being faced with inflated prices.
What happened? The Minister of Veterans Affairs is probably aware of the fact that many veterans who wanted to buy land were advised by the Department of Veterans Affairs to wait until prices fell before buying land and equipment. In some cases they advised the veterans to wait for two years and in the meantime to work on farms to gain experience. What happened? In those two years, from 1946 to 1948, the price of a John Deere tractor increased from $1,800 to $2,800, and the price of land also soared. The result was that those veterans who had been advised by the department to hold off buying land and equipment had to pay 30 or 40 per cent more for what they wanted. In many cases the grants under the Veterans Land Act were swallowed up by the inflation that had occurred. I am sure that the government must feel deeply concerned about these men who could not help themselves.
Not even satisfied with that, apparently they are going to make the men in the armed services who are overseas pay income tax. However, I would be out of order if I discussed income tax at the present time.
I should like the parliamentary assistant to deal with the point as to whether or not these taxes are in reality a tax upon a large proportion of the savings of the people in the lower income groups who are not able to meet the high cost of living out of current income and are having to draw upon savings. This has been going on to quite an extent. I notice the February 1951 issue of the Canadian Statistical Review, at page five, states:
The increase in consumer expenditure was the principal factor accounting for a decline of four per cent in personal saving, from $802 million in 1949 to $769 million in 1950. If changes in farm inventories are deducted from the saving figures, a much greater decline in the rate of saving is indicated. Thus, personal saving, exclusive of changes in farm inventories, was $604 million in 1950, compared' with $875 million in 1949, which represents five per cent of personal income in 1950 compared with seven per cent in 1949.
As the situation deteriorates still further it means that not only will people not be able to save as much, they will actually have to draw upon their savings to meet the current cost of living, if they are lucky enough to have savings. We all know that there are many people who have already liquidated their savings. I know from personal experience and contact with many people that today they are cashing their bonds and various other capital assets in order to meet

current expenditures. In other words, they are living on capital rather than on current income.
As a result of this resolution they are now going to have to pay an additional tax on the savings they spend. I think the minister should deal with that point because it is a very undesirable feature.

This sales tax attacks the municipalities, who are not profit-making corporations, in the same way as it attacks profit-making corporations. The municipalities-the government of the country just the same as the federal government-are rendering service to the people, doing a lot of development work and! carrying a lot-of social services, which are rendered directly to the individual. If it is impossible to take the sales tax off such things as the machinery bought by the municipalities, then the government should give a grant in lieu of this tax to every municipality in Canada of 1,000 inhabitants or more.
During the afternoon and early evening we have heard a good deal of argument in reference to the impact of this tax on the families of this nation. The argument put forward so far has dealt largely with the increased cost of clothing and the various supplies required in a home, but I should like to direct attention to the fact that municipal costs are likewise paid largely by the homemakers. Every cent of the sales tax on supplies purchased by a municipality is paid out of real estate taxes or in rent, which has a direct relationship to real estate taxes, by those in this country least able to pay. No doubt hon. members are well aware that it has long been the contention of the association of mayors and reeves that the sales tax should be remitted on supplies purchased by municipalities, whether those supplies are machinery, hospital supplies, articles required by boards of education, or whatever they may be. In whatever category they may fall they are paid for by the people of the municipalities through increased real estate taxes.
I am sure hon. members have followed, as I have, the reports in the papers during the last couple of months. There may be some municipality in some obscure corner of this country that has lowered its taxes this year,

but if so I have not noticed it. Almost every municipality has increased its tax rate to a substantial extent. I believe this house is indebted to the hon. member for Acadia for the light he has thrown on the effects of the budget proposals which are now before us. I believe many hon. members did not realize what would be the result when these various changes are put into effect. It seems to me that the Minister of Finance and his advisers should hang their heads in shame when they appreciate the effect this will have on the common working people of this country. Perhaps it is all right to sit in this chamber, to eat in our restaurant up on the sixth floor, to live at a big hotel here or in another city, and charge plenty for a day's work or for a half hour's work; but compare that with the conditions under which the little fellow has to live and the pay he draws for a full day's work. I believe these things should be taken into consideration before we proceed further with the budget proposals.
Many say the people like taxes. That is not the case; but apparently a lot of people go to sleep when election day comes around, because they keep putting the Liberals back into office. Then they have to pay heavier taxes and live on reduced earnings. But when the next election comes around they put the Liberals right back in, as I believe they have done today in Prince Edrward Island. I do not know why they do it. If I were a Liberal and had to support a thing like this budget, which many of them including the hon. member for Mackenzie do not believe in, I would get out of the Liberal party and stay out for good. Section 4 of these proposals reads:

Mr. Chairman, I feel that the parliamentary assistant would like to be answering some questions. I know he is most

desirous of answering a number of questions that have been asked of him, so I shall not make any lengthy speech at this time. I am most surprised that the members on the government side have not had something to say about this addition to the general sales tax. If ever there was an unjust and unconscionable tax to be imposed at a time of inflation, it is this additional two per cent. It is insidious and is resorted to because it is hidden. It has already resulted in an increase in the cost of living. It has done so in the case of gasoline and clothing. Shoes are going up, and all because of the fact that the government has joined in the merry-go-round of self-created inflation, its own home-made variety, by adding an extra two per cent. There is no amount of explaining that can get away from the fact that this tax is adding to the cost of living in this country, whatever the brain trust that advises the government may say. They find it an easy way to advise the government to take this means. I am not going to quote what other finance ministers have said, but I do point out that, at a time when the cost of living is going up as never before, the government adds to the speed of the merry-go-round by a sales tax. It does add to the cost of living. It does not affect those whose income is over $3,000 a year to the same extent that it does those whose income is under that, as the member for Hamilton West pointed out a moment ago.
There are a number of matters on which I desire information from the parliamentary assistant, and I am sure he will be able to answer because the dominion bureau of statistics has furnished some information in this regard. I should like to ask him how many dollars a year the ordinary family, covered by and comprised within the computation made in arriving at the cost of living, will have to pay in sales tax this year by reason of the addition of two per cent. I am speaking of the family with an income under $3,000 per year, for after all they are the ones that are generally taken into consideration in arriving at the index figures connected with the cost of living. I have endeavoured to compute this, and I think it comes to about $39 for a family per year.
Then, take the other items. How much will it cost such an ordinary family in respect of those goods covered by section 2, the excise tax on goods mentioned in schedule I? What will the cost be to this ordinary family, which I believe comprises four and a half persons, the average number that is taken into consideration in connection with the index number? How much will it cost them in respect of paragraph 4, the fifteen per cent excise tax on stoves, hot plates, grills, washing machines, refrigerators and the like? If we
Excise Tax Act
have that information we then have some idea as to the effect of these taxes. Certainly, these taxes are not going to be anti-inflationary. Their purpose can only be to secure revenue, their result a reduction in the ordinary standard of living among those in the lower income tax brackets.
I am going to give the minister an opportunity, before I say any more, to furnish the committee with this information because I am sure he has it all available. After all, before taxes such as these would be imposed by the cabinet, there must have been information secured from the bureau of statistics. I do not want to take up more time in this debate than is necessary, but I have a fair list of questions here which have been asked. First of all, however, I should like to reaffirm the position so far as sales tax and income tax are concerned. In the last year or so I have read back the budget speeches of every minister of finance since the end of the last war. I believe they have all faced this problem. Every minister of finance has agreed that the income tax is undoubtedly the fairest tax, and from the point of view of the lecturer in the classroom that it is the only fair tax. There is, however, a great difference between an academic discussion on taxes and the actual application to an issue. Every country has found there is a very practical limit so far as the application of income tax is concerned.
I am not going to quote any economic authority, but I am going to quote my little Scotch friend the hon. member for Selkirk. Three or four years ago he put a remark on Hansard which shows so well the reaction of people to an excessive income tax. You will remember that during the last war we had an income tax scale much heavier than we do now, and we had much lower exemptions. The income tax laws were beginning to be applied to farmers. My friend protested very bitterly about the extension of income tax to them, and told how a farmer in his riding had given up dairy cows and was going to continue as a wheat farmer. This farmer had said, "I willna milk cows for Ilsley"; that is the very effect of an aggressive income tax. In my own riding during the war we saw its effect in the form of absenteeism in the shipyards. Once a man's income got to the level where extra work put him in a high

Excise Tax Act
bracket, he said it was not worth while working. They have certainly had that same experience in Britain.
Some of you will recall that last spring I had the opportunity of going around Europe in connection with the collection of war debts. I was quite impressed with a talk I had with the minister of finance of Belgium. The Belgians have recovered more quickly than any other European people. They have worked very hard. He said that one of the incentives they had given the people to work hard was a low income tax rate. The people who worked overtime got most of the extra money, and spent it on consumer goods which were taxed. It is true that the Belgian government got more revenue by means of much heavier excise taxes and sales taxes than the British had. In Britain they have a very heavy income tax rate. When a man did have a little money left after income taxes, he found there was nothing on which he could spend it. He could not buy more food because it was rationed, more clothing because it was rationed. He could not get extra material to extend his house, because it was in short supply. A government is faced with the hard fact that, if it cannot rely solely on corporation and income taxes for raising revenues which it needs, there is a very practical limitation.
During the last two or three years hon. members will recall that there has been no absence of suggestions from opposition members for more Pacific pacts, more Colombo plans, and for bigger national defence expenditures; all those things have to be paid for. Turning to the practical point of diminishing returns, as to not just taxes but productivity throughout this nation, it can be fairly quickly reached and it would be reached overnight if we tried to impose the entire load of taxation on income tax. Since this country has had both income taxes and indirect taxes, we have had to try to maintain this almost even balance between our collections of direct tax and our collections of indirect tax.

The income tax of this country has of course a direct relation to our tax program. I have here a table which I intended to put on the record when we were discussing the personal income tax. It is one showing that this country has higher income

tax exemptions than have the other two countries with whom we can reasonably compare ourselves, namely, the United States and Great Britain. Here in Canada we have income tax exemptions as follows: for a single man $1,000; for a married man, $2,000. Perhaps I should go right across the board. For a single man, $1,000 in Canada; $600 in the United States and $319 in the United Kingdom. That is at $2.90 to the pound. The United Kingdom will show one or two other provisions which I will mention when I come to the table. Exemptions for a married man: in Canada, $2,000; in the United States, $1,200 and in the United Kingdom $551. Children receiving family allowances are given exemptions of $150. If they are not in receipt of family allowance, they are given exemptions of $400. There is no family allowance in the United States. Children get a $600 exemption. In Britain, whether the child receives family allowance or not, he receives an exemption of $203. The family allowance in Britain is taxable. The British allow a further exemption of 20 per cent on earned income.
I want to give a specific example. I said a little earlier this afternoon that today in Canada we have 5,200,000 people gainfully employed, of whom only 2,200,000 pay income tax. That is because of these high levels of exemptions. I will take the example of a man earning $3,000 a year, because that was the figure mentioned by one of the speakers.

Mr. Chairman, I think the parliamentary assistant is going to have a rather difficult time in convincing the people that this extra tax is not going to materially

Excise Tax Act
raise prices. The people who buy these things are going to be the best judges. A while ago somebody said that the ratepayers of the country had voted in the Liberal government. I have not much sympathy with those people who would put in a government like this. I would say that all those who voted Liberal deserve just what they are getting.
A while ago the parliamentary assistant said that the reason they did not increase the tax on liquor was that it had reached the point of diminishing return. I think almost everyone in this house will agree that that tax should have been increased instead of the tax on some other things. The parliamentary assistant said also that they did not want to encroach upon provincial jurisdiction. I think both these reasons are exceedingly wrong.
In the first place the federal government is already taxing liquor so there would be no question of their getting into that business -they are already in it. It is just a matter of degree, a matter of how much further they want to go with a tax on liquor. Apart from its use for medicinal purposes, if there ever was a luxury, the use of liquor is one. I think it is safe to say that with all the taxes that have been put on liquor there has been no sign of a lessened consumption. The provincial governments have used this tax as a successful source of revenue. I am just speaking from memory, but I think Alberta got something like $12 million and there was an increase in consumption. This shows that there is a field here for increased taxation by the federal government.
Then it was said that taxation on liquor had reached the point where it was encouraging bootlegging. That is not a very good argument. The government has increased the tax on tobacco and cigarettes to the point where it has caused a material increase in bootlegging and blackmarketing. Yet you hear no suggestion from the federal government that they are going to eliminate these taxes-I am not suggesting that they should -in order to stop bootlegging. I am just pointing out the impracticability of suggesting that they have reached the point of diminishing return with liquor but not with tobacco and cigarettes. I noticed in the paper the other day that Ontario is having an exceedingly difficult time in curtailing bootlegging and blackmarketing of cigarettes, and only yesterday the papers stated that British Columbia was facing the same problem.
I have not heard of any greater difficulty in the bootlegging of liquor now than there was before. Yet all of a sudden there is this surge

of bootlegging and blackmarketing of cigarettes. I think the argument of the government that they could not raise the tax on liquor because it had reached the point of diminishing return and would increase bootlegging and blackmarketing is not very well founded.
I think the people generally who consume these articles would far rather have the tax increased on them than have an increase on the tax on these other things which enter into the ordinary necessities of life. The idea of taxing washing machines! The parliamentary assistant says that that is the only way they can get revenue. That is not the only reason the Minister of Finance gave when he was giving his speech. If I remember rightly he gave as a reason, first, that they had to get revenue and, second, that they had to save material for use in rearmament and so on.
That reminds me of the last war when they began to raise the price of automobiles. It was said that one reason for doing that was to save material so that it could go into the manufacture of armaments. When we suggested that the proper way to handle it was by rationing the government replied that they could not do that. The same thing applies today. If we need the metal which goes into washing machines, refrigerators and automobiles so urgently for war purposes, the proper thing to do is to ration these articles and treat everybody fairly.
This is not a fair tax because those with large incomes are going to get automobiles, washing machines or refrigerators when they want them. An extra $50 or $60 on a washing machine or a refrigerator, or another $200, $300, $400 or $500 on an automobile will not amount to a row of beans to those in the higher income brackets. But it is of material importance to the housewife who needs a new washing machine. Perhaps the parliamentary assistant knows of cases, but I never heard of a housewife buying a new electric washing machine if she did not need it pretty badly.
We are told that there is to be no tax on those that are operated by hand. I doubt if any of them are being made, although there may be one or two. The country is becoming electrified so rapidly that only electrical machines are used. If not electrical, then the gasoline machine is purchased. I do not think anyone would suggest that a farm wife will buy a washing machine as a luxury.
One thing that has amused me all down through the years that I have been here since 1935 is that I have heard it said repeatedly that the fairest tax was the income tax. I do

not think I have heard anyone say this session that the income tax was not the fairest tax. If that is so, and I believe it is, we should look to that field, and in saying this I am bearing in mind what the parliamentary assistant said a moment ago about discouraging production and all that sort of thing.
The very fact that the exemption on income tax is set at $2,000 for married persons indicates that we consider that everyone having an income of less than $2,000 is not in position to pay income tax and maintain a decent standard of living. With the present runaway inflation that $2,000 will not buy $2,000 worth of goods, it will buy only a little over one-half. The parliamentary assistant pointed out that this tax was to raise money. If that is so, why try to get blood out of a stone, why try to get money out of those people who are less able to pay income tax? The exemptions from that tax clearly indicate the position. When you look over the income tax field you find that the greatest amount of revenue is obtained from those people with incomes between $3,000 and $8,000. Certainly everyone will recognize the fact that nowadays an income of $3,000 does not keep a family in a position where they can live in luxury.

Mr. Chairman, I agree one hundred per cent with what has been said by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. I find it exceedingly hard to understand the explanation made by the parliamentary assistant for not imposing a tax on alcoholic spirits. It seems to be based on an idea that the tax on liquor has reached the point of diminishing return, and that idea seems to be based on a statement made by Premier Frost with regard to the situation in Ontario.

If that is the case, there must be in Ontario some indication that the consumption of liquor or the sale of liquor has been diminished by the latest tax that was applied to it, namely, the one imposed last September. I think that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, on investigation, will find that not only did the sale of liquor in Ontario not decrease since the imposition of the last tax in September, 1950, but that it has actually gone up since that time. I can see no indication at all that the tax return from the sale of alcoholic spirits has reached the point of diminishing return. I can see no reason why that tax should not be applied. I would like to hear a fuller explanation from the parliamentary assistant as to how the Department of Finance has arrived at the conclusion that the tax that can be obtained from alcoholic spirits has reached the point of diminishing return.

speechtext:
I cannot do more than repeat what has been said by the Minister of Finance in this respect. Our tax on liquor is a tax which has never been cut back. During the war it was the first tax to be increased, and increased sharply. In the period since the war we have not cut back the tax on alcoholic liquor at all. The first tax we hit in the baby budget last fall was the tax on liquor, followed by that on corporations. The baby budget was the first of our defence budgets.
The breakdown I put on the record last week gives hon. members some idea of the rate of taxation on liquor. When a bottle of liquor which is sold by a distiller for $1.10- and that includes the profit, and the cost of operation of the plant, and the land tax, and all the ordinary local taxes faced by any manufacturer-retails for $4.25 across the country, bearing in mind the combination of the federal tax and the amount put on by the provincial liquor control board, you have some idea of the very heavy present taxation on liquor.
The fact that Premier Frost made that statement before the budget was brought down serves to confirm the fact that the Department of National Revenue had come to the conclusion that we were getting pretty close to the limit, in terms of taxation on liquor as related to other taxes. Of course that is always the relationship we must keep in mind. The question of the enforcement of the law was one brought up, not just by Premier Frost, but on other occasions by other provincial leaders.
I think some hon. members are confusing the situation as it applies to cigarettes and
Excise Tax Act
to liquor. The manufacture of liquor is a comparatively simple operation. When there is too great a disparity between the actual cost of manufacture and the sale price, there is a natural incentive for illegal manufacture. On the other hand there is not the same opportunity for the illegal manufacture of cigarettes. The problem we have to contend with in that instance is the one of smuggling from the United States.
In view of the fact that liquor taxes have never been cut back, were the first to be increased last fall, and the fact that it is the belief of the Department of National Revenue that we were reaching the limit of taxation, so far as revenue from liquor was concerned-even without confirmation from Premier Frost in the Ontario legislature- we decided not to raise the liquor tax at this session.
Then, the hon. member for Fraser Valley referred to margarine. I would say that margarine is one of the few food products we tax. There is a ten per cent sales tax on margarine. Then, the other questions I had anticipated he would ask, the duties on imported edible oils, I shall deal with when we come to the customs tariff item.
The hon. member asked for information showing the revenue produced by the increase in the taxation on cigarettes and tobacco. On cigarettes, in a full year, the increase will add $26 million of revenue, and in the fiscal year 1951-52, $21 million. As hon. members know, receipts lag behind the period on which the tax is imposed. Then, on tobacco in a full year it will be $17 million, and this year $14 million.

I have listened with a good deal of interest to the statement by the parliamentary assistant that liquor is now bearing a tax sufficiently high. I say to him and to the committee that, in my opinion, if the tax on liquor is high, then the sales tax on the necessities of life, so far as the great masses of the people are concerned1, is more oppressive than any tax on liquor could possibly be.
I think the hon. member for Fraser Valley is quite right when he -says that those who wish to drink liquor will buy it, no matter what the cost. I believe that was clearly demonstrated during the war, as to some extent he pointed out. I remember being in Edmonton and being told that those who came

Excise Tax Act
in on a Saturday night from the Alaska highway, and wanted to buy a bottle of liquor, were prepared to pay bellboys as high as $40 for a bottle of it.
Consequently I do not follow the argument made by the parliamentary assistant or the minister. Indeed, I would read a description of another budget, which I think would be of interest, and which objects to the increase in the high cost of living:
Meanwhile, the profiteers escape, the excess profits tax is reduced. No attempt is made to tax the huge fortunes accumulated during the war, and every year it will become more difficult to make an inventory of such fortunes and compel them to contribute to the public revenue. By passing the conscription law parliament declared that every man's life was at the service of the state. Surely if that is right, it is even more certain that every man's fortune should be at the service of the state. Still more is it true that the state should have the right to take at least a share of fortunes accumulated by men out of the very necessities of war, by men who were safe and comfortable at home while young Canadians were suffering and dying in the trenches. The government lets these accumulators of fortunes go free, while it taxes the veteran on his clothing and his boots.
Who said that? Well, here it is-"The Liberal Point of View," June, 1920. And the budget? The Drayton budget of that year.
