I want to protest against the sales tax, and the tax on necessities such as stoves and refrigerators, and other appliances required in an apartment house. I would point out to the parliamentary assistant that last year New Brunswick imposed a provincial sales tax of four per cent and the increase in the dominion sales tax will bring that other tax up to about six per cent. With the wholesaler and retailer markups on the four per cent tax, the retail price of many necessities of life is up about 20 to 25 per cent, in some cases up to 50 per cent. There are tremendous markups, both wholesale and retail, on articles such as drugs.
The parliamentary assistant talked about a bottle of liquor costing the store about $1.10, whereas the consumer had to pay $4 for the same bottle. That is a tremendous profit. Let the provincial governments reduce their profits. A few years ago we thought it was an awful thing for a government to be selling liquor, and I do not think they should today. subtopic: PERCENTAGE OF FAMILY INCOME SPENT ON MAJOR CONSUMER ITEMS SUBJECT TO SALES TAX FOR VARIOUS INCOME GROUPS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to increase the cost of refrigerators and articles of that kind to the purchaser by increasing the sales tax is in my opinion nothing less than scandalous. The extravagant spending by this government reminds me of a true story I heard some years ago. Two prospectors discovered one of the first producing mines in the Kirkland Lake district. They were brothers and I am sure that any mining men in the house will recognize these men when they hear the story. They sold out their interest to an English syndicate, each man receiving around $200,000. As these brothers admitted to me years later, they were not used to money and they squandered it quite quickly. Each of them bought a Cadillac car; one built a race track near Niagara Falls while the other tried to farm up in the frozen north.
One day the two brothers and another prospector, a co-discoverer of the mine, were proceeding down the main highway from Kirkland Lake in one of the Cadillacs.

The car was well oiled and, according to the brothers, all the men in the car were well oiled. They approached an old farmer carrying two buckets of water. As the Cadillac approached he stood dumbfounded at the side of the road and just as they passed him he threw up the buckets of water and said, "Go to it, you fools".
When I think of the extravagant spending of this government I am reminded of that story of the two prospectors who had so much money that they did not know what to do with it. Unfortunately in the last two elections the people of Canada have been something like this farmer. They have simply thrown up the buckets of water and said, "Go to it". But the day is coming when the farmers and all the voters of Canada will not just throw up buckets of water, they will mark their ballots as a token of the fact that they realize that this government is building houses that are costing hundreds of thousands of dollars too much and is squandering the people's money and actually depriving the public of refrigerators.
I think of the young married man who cannot afford to buy a house and who must move into an apartment. If this man had a home in the country he might have a hole in the ground where he could keep his food from decaying or rotting, but apartment dwellers must of necessity have refrigerators which must be supplied by themselves or by the owner. You cannot run out to the backyard of an apartment and (pick up kindling and some firewood. It is not likely they are living over a coal mine like the people in Edmonton, and the result is they must buy electric stoves and electric refrigerators.
Undoubtedly the parliamentary assistant will take all the credit, if there is any credit due, for the raising of these large sums of money which will be necessary if we come to an all-out war. The former minister of finance certainly took all the credit for the financial brains he had behind him, for all the theatrical people and the moving picture celebrities who helped, for the greatest advertising agencies in the world which put on a campaign to raise money for the war. Yet one great almighty man, the minister of finance of that time, stuck out his chest and said, "Look, I did it all with my little hatchet".
The other night the parliamentary assistant made a speech and he waved a piece of paper around trying to explain why his department did this or did that. I believe he certainly would like to take all the credit in the world,
Excise Tax Act
if there is any credit due to the government. In my opinion there is not very much credit due.
The government says that they cannot tax liquor. A few moments ago an hon. member mentioned that people had paid bootleggers up to $40 per bottle, and during prohibition days in New York were willing to pay $25. In Toronto, in the King Edward hotel or the Royal York hotel, you find people paying $8, $10 and $15 a bottle. When the legal places of sale and the cocktail bars close, people who want liquor go out and buy it from bootleggers and are ready to absorb the increased price. I believe the man who wants liquor will be prepared to pay a higher price at the legal places of sale. I believe the people who want cigarettes are paying the increased taxation right here in Ottawa.
I think every effort should have been made to keep down the cost of essentials to the home owners and to the home seekers. A fraction of a cent or one or two cents on cigarettes is not a great deal to the individual, but when it is all lumped together a tremendous burden is placed on the people of Canada by this excessive sales tax. There are people who do not want to debauch themselves with liquor or who smoke with moderation, and yet they are having to pay much more for essentials. Liquor is not an essential, it is a luxury.
I cannot conceive how the parliamentary assistant can stand up in this House of Commons and say that they have fully considered the question of increasing the tax on liquor, and yet they placed increased taxes on refrigerators and other essentials. The two things just do not go together. The parliamentary assistant may flourish a piece of paper in the air, but no matter how much he may try to explain what the government has done, I do not think he can successfully explain it to the people of Canada. I am positive that at the next election the voters of Canada will assert themselves in no uncertain terms. They will show that their eyes have now been opened and they will no longer throw up two buckets of water. They will mark their ballots accordingly to express their disapproval of this government.

Mr. Chairman, you are an optimist. I should like to say a word about a point which the hon. member for Lake Centre put to the parliamentary assistant in the form of a set of questions. My hope is that the parliamentary assistant will look into that phase of the matter and give us a little more explicit answer on a later occasion. The hon. member for Lake Centre raised the question as to how much the cost of living of an average family-he defined an average family as a family having an income of less than $3,000 a year-would be affected by the increased taxes set out in the Excise Tax Act resolution now before us. I think the parliamentary assistant had difficulty understanding the question at first. When he did get it he was not sure that his department would be able to provide the information.
May I point out, as has been indicated previously in this debate, that before we had the budget debate the house was engaged in a debate on the cost of living. It was suggested to us by the government that debate was inopportune at that time, that we should wait for the budget, that the budget would deal with the problem. That seems to me to suggest that before taxes of this kind were imposed the government should have considered their effect on the cost of living. Maybe the government is prepared to defend that effect, but at least they should have been prepared to tell us what the effect is. The hon. member for Lake Centre referred to the average family as being a family with something less than $3,000 a year. I am afraid the average family in my constituency has considerably less than that to live on during a year.
I	do know that the cost of living index is worked out on the basis of what has happened to the cost of a basket of goods and services which in the base period of 1935-
Excise Tax Act
39 cost $1,453 a year. As the parliamentary assistant knows, at that time the bureau of statistics took a certain basket of goods and services which added up to that figure. Now they ascertain what those same goods and services cost at today's prices.
This means that each increase of $14.53 per year in the cost of living of an average family means an increase of one point in the cost of living index. The 'hon. member for Lake Centre did some rough figuring of his own before he spoke tonight, and said he thought the taxes set out in this act would cost the average family around $39 a year. That is the sort of figure I think the Department of Finance should have obtained before it imposed these taxes. If it did not, then it should now obtain it and tell us what the figure is before we vote on this resolution. If the hon. member for Lake Centre is correct and that figure is around $39 a year, or we will say $40 dr $45 a year, right there you have the basis for an increase of three points in the cost of living index. It may take a little time for that increase to be reflected in the index issued by the bureau of statistics, but it will be felt by our people right away. If the parliamentary assistant is not able to deal with that phase of the matter tonight I hope he will go into it very fully before we get back to this resolution on another occasion. I have not had a chance to look at the table he said he put on Hansard today. Certainly I will look at it when we get Hansard tomorrow, but I doubt if that table answers the kind of question put by the hon. member for Lake Centre, and which I am putting in a slightly different form now.
Another comment I wanted to make about the sales tax, which is covered in one paragraph of this resolution, is that it seems to me the parliamentary assistant let the cat out of the bag this afternoon. When complaints about this tax were being made from this side of the house the parliamentary assistant pointed out, as I remember his figures, that there were in Canada some
5.200.000	wage earners, of whom only
2.200.000	pay income tax. His point, and in fact I think he said it quite clearly, was that we need a tax of this kind so that other group of 3,000,000 wage earners would be taxed to help pay the cost of such social services as family allowances and old age pensions.
I	wish to draw to the attention of the government two points which respect to that admission by the parliamentary assistant this afternoon. On the one hand it is an admission that these taxes will be borne heavily by people in the lower brackets. The Minister

Excise Tax Act
of Finance tried to make a great deal, during the course of his budget speech, out of the argument that because so many things did not bear the sales tax the people in the lower brackets pay that tax on only a limited percentage of the goods they buy. Well, the parliamentary assistant cannot have it both ways. He cannot say on the one hand that the poor people do not have to pay this tax, and on the other hand that they are applying the tax so the people who do not pay income tax will pay their share of the cost of social services such as old age pensions and family allowances. The fact is that they do have to pay it.
The other point I wish to make is that it seems to me this is practising deception. The government makes a great deal out of the fact that it has certain exemptions with regard to the income tax below which people do not have to pay that tax. I say they would be far better off if there were no sales tax whatsoever, even if the exemptions were lowered, so people would be taxed according to their ability to pay instead of being taxed at these high levels on the necessities of life without regard to their ability to pay. I submit that it is practising deception to say these people are exempt from the payment of income tax and then turn around1 and impose taxes upon them in this way, which the parliamentary assistant said; today was the purpose of this sales tax.
I do not like jumping around in this resolution from paragraph 1 to paragraph 4 to paragraph 7, and so on.

Of course this whole absurd practice began back in 1948, when on one occasion they were caught short in the house and lost a vote. I want to register my protest, along with others who have spoken today, against this tax being imposed on such basic-necessities as electric stoves, electric washing machines, and electric refrigerators. I hope the parliamentary assistant enjoyed reading the editorial in this evening's Ottawa Journal, in which he is referred to as Grandfather Sinclair. If he has read the editorial I am sure he blushed at the picture it painted of him when it said that while he is still a young man he would like to suggest to the young people of today that they start life not with the things regarded today as necessities but with the limited conveniences our grandparents had a generation or two ago. On another occasion, as a matter of fact, I will introduce another amendment to this omnibus eight point resolution. My amendment will deal with this paragraph 4. It seems to me that an alternative might be suggested which would be much better than trying to raise $16 million in this way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speechtext:
Naturally, in raising this extra money, every possible avenue of taxation was carefully explored by the budget committee. The United States has a capital gains tax, in the administration of which they have encountered certain problems. In view of their experience and our own system of taxation, it was not thought practical to introduce such a system. We have always regarded the best tax as being a tax on income rather than a tax on capital.
As I pointed out earlier, our whole tax policy is along the lines of the British system rather than the United States system. The British have not got a capital gains tax, although one year they had the income tax rate so high in the upper brackets that in some instances they actually took more in taxes than the person had in income. That was done only once, so far as I know.
